newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: WEEKAHEAD - Australian markets focused on GDP.
newsitem.headline: WEEKAHEAD - Australian markets focused on GDP.

text.p: March quarter Gross Domestic Product (GDP) data stands out as the major economic event of the week but Reserve Bank's decision to cut interest rates on May 23 has taken some of the heat out of the figures.

Quarterly growth is expected to pick up from the 0.5 percent pace of the December quarter, but because last March's strong 1.6 percent rise drops out of annual calculations, the annual rate of GDP will slow to under 2.5 percent for the first time since the year to September 1993, economists said.
While consumption and income are expected to be strong in the March quarter, a large detraction from stocks and some weakness in company profits is expected to detract from GDP.

However, in the wake of the rate cut the national accounts are essentially historical, providing a snapshot of the economy at the end of March and not telling markets too much about the prospects for further rate moves.
And on those prospects, economists still remain reluctant to call another cut. A Reuters survey on Friday found only one economist seeing a better than even chance of another rate cut.

A number of economists putting a 40 percent chance on a rate cut who said the bias to their forecasts was to the topside, and would depend heavily on how the activity indicators, mainly employment, pans out over the next few months.
"If unemployment looks set to stay above 8.5 percent and the Australian dollar is resilient, then there will be another rate cut," said Westpac Banking Corp chief economist Nigel Stapledon.
The RBA board meets on Tuesday.
"We doubt the RBA will move rates on Wednesday," Colonial State Bank group economist Hans Kunnen said.
"However, if we see more economic weakness, a rate cut in July is a strong possibility."

Rothschild economists also saw little chance of a cut following the meeting. "We rate the chance of a rate cut as about 20 percent, given that last week's cut was a conditional one ... and that there are still some signs of recovery on the horizon," the economists said in a commentary.

The most important of the upcoming indicators will be next week's employment data but markets will be looking for clues for the speech RBA Governor Ian Macfarlane gives at a Westpac Economic conference in London on Thursday.

The speech will be presented early morning Friday Australian time and given the way the market apparently misread his statements earlier this month, it will be interesting to see the reaction if Macfarlane appears overly bullish or bearish.
Of lesser significance this week are April building approvals data on Monday and net foreign debt on Tuesday.
AUSTRALIAN BONDS (Fri: 10-yr cash 7.46 pct, 3-yr 6.18 pct
The debt market remains in bullish mood, and will no doubt be thinking about the possibility of a further easing.
This positive mood is in response to last week's data showing a sharp drop in April retail trade, which was the first consecutive fall in the series for some four years.

Yields at the short-end of the bond curve dropped to their lowest level since early 1994 on the data and bill futures started to price in the chance of another easing by September on Friday and push out any chance of a tightening until March 1998.

The long-end is still vulnerable to moves in the United States, which remains overhung by the possibilty of a tightening, and will be holding its breath in front of next Friday's May U.S. labour force report.
U.S. Treasuries closed higher for the second straight day on Friday on technical factors and hopes the economy will continue to show moderate growth in the second quarter.
The 30-year bond closed with a yield of 6.92 percent, down from 6.98 percent the previous day.
"Australian bond yields can fall, period," said Colonial State Bank's Kunnen. "They are currently the highest in the industrialised world despite our sound economic fundamentals."
AUSTRALIAN DOLLAR (Fri: US$0.7604/09, NY $0.7598/03)
The dollar looks set to remain under pressure this week as the market frets over the chance of yet another rate cut.

The currency has fallen over 1-1/2 cents since the last easing on May 23 and an attempted recovery last week was stillborn when retail sales data proved surprisingly weak. That saw the currency finish at a three month low of US$0.7706 as domestic interest rates moved well below those offered by the U.S. dollar for the first time in more than a decade.
The outlook for monetary policy should dominate this week.
Analysts generally doubted the bank would ease again so soon but given the market had been surprised by three of the last four cuts, it would still be tense come Wednesday morning.
Even if the bank holds steady, traders expected the currency to test the depth of exporter support at 76 cents and saw a risk of reaching the 1997 low of US$0.7550 made in February.
"Following the monetary policy easing just a week ago, many expected the AUD to take a king hit - but it never came," Deutsche Morgan Grenfell economists said in a commentary.

"Despite the currency's resilience this past week the Aussie lower in the near term. The most notable of these are increasing market focus on the chances of another monetary policy easing and the continued outperformance of the Australian bond market."
"However, in the medium term we still view the major risks on the currency as being on the upside."
STOCKS (Fri: All Ordinaries index 2610.5, up 19.9)
The steep upward trajectory of the Australian share market is set to continue with a bullish bourse finishing last week in record breaking form.
While Friday's turnover was inflated by May series option exercise, residual turnover was still within a whisker of A$1 billion, a thumping display of bullish intent.
In numbers terms, the All Ordinaries has rocketed 11 percent since April 1 and brokers said the market was likely to see more of the same. However, buyers are being selective.

Brokers said only a dramatic correction on Wall Street was likely to reverse sentiment. The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed just little changed on Friday after an early sell-off of 88 points afer a surprise profit warning by Intel.

"It could on on with it. I think our market will hold even if Wall Street fell a 100 points or so," said Grant Williams of Reynolds and Co. "If Wall Street had a bigger fall or did it over a few nights, then maybe we will come back."
Corporate events this week include Macquarie Bank annual results on Monday. Building materials group James Hardie and whitegoods manufacturer Email both reportt full year results on Thursday.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
